description: Im a teen who has a strong passion for aerospace engineering and physics. I decided to create a team for the NASA Challenge because I love solving problems, and learning new things about space and technology. This challenge is a great opportunity for me to combine my interests, develop my skills, and turn ideas into something meaningful.
summary:
NASA Lunar Mk.1 is an interactive space exploration and mission-planning platform combining 3D Solar System visualization, NASA/JPL scientific datasets, and orbital mechanics.

Users can explore planetary positions, investigate lunar terrain using LOLA elevation data, analyze craters and slopes, identify potential landing sites, and plan rover routes based on distance and terrain difficulty.

The Earth–Moon Mission Planner applies mathematical physics, including Hohmann transfer equations, gravitational parameters, orbital velocities, delta-v calculations, and transfer times, to simulate spacecraft trajectories and evaluate mission requirements.

Additional features include lunar sunlight analysis, Earth–Moon communication visibility, planetary orbit visualization, and exploration of planetary characteristics.

The project integrates scientific resources from NASA/JPL Horizons, LOLA, MOLA, MESSENGER, Magellan, NASA planetary fact sheets, and Cassini and New Horizons mission imagery.

My goal is to connect theoretical physics with practical space exploration through accessible, interactive tools that inspire and support safer, smarter future lunar missions.
details:
NASA Lunar Mk.1 – Interactive Space Exploration & Mission Planning

NASA Lunar Mk.1 is a space exploration and mission-planning application that combines an interactive 3D Solar System, real scientific datasets, terrain analysis, and mathematical physics.

How it works: Users can explore the Sun, eight planets, Pluto, and the Moon in 3D, change dates to observe planetary positions and rotations, and switch between overview and physical-scale visualizations. The lunar exploration system uses NASA LRO/LOLA elevation data to visualize craters and terrain. Users can select landing locations, create multiple waypoints, and calculate rover routes using terrain elevation, slope, and distance.

The mission-planning system implements orbital mechanics, including Hohmann transfers, bi-elliptic transfers, Lambert solutions, and gravitational swing-by calculations. It calculates trajectory parameters, orbital velocities, transfer times, and delta-v requirements. Special and general relativity calculations also explore time dilation and gravitational redshift. Additional features include lunar sunlight analysis and estimated direct-to-Earth communication visibility.

Benefits and intended impact: The application makes complex astronomical concepts and orbital mechanics interactive and understandable. It connects theoretical physics with practical exploration scenarios and helps users investigate challenges involving lunar landing locations, rover mobility, spacecraft transfers, and communication conditions.

Technology: I developed the project individually using JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, and Python. Three.js powers the 3D environment, while Node.js supports numerical testing. Playwright and Puppeteer are used for browser testing, and Capacitor provides Android integration.

Creativity and considerations: The creative aspect is combining several normally separate disciplines into one interactive environment: planetary science, orbital mechanics, relativity, terrain intelligence, and mission planning. During development, I considered scientific accuracy, physical units, realistic scale, computational limitations, usability, and the reliability of external datasets. I also distinguish approximate simulations from precise NASA ephemeris-based calculations.

My goal is to make space science more accessible and inspire people to understand, explore, and contribute to humanity's future beyond Earth.
